Rhapsody in Blue is a 1924 musical composition for solo piano and jazz band by George Gershwin. The composition is known for its integration of jazz rhythms with classical music, and premiered on February 12, 1924, as part of bandleader Paul Whiteman's "An Experiment in Modern Music" concert.

The composition was originally titled "American Rhapsody," but Gershwin's brother Ira suggested the title "Rhapsody in Blue" after seeing an exhibit of paintings by James McNeill Whistler.

The Rhapsody in Blue established Gershwin's reputation as a serious composer and has since become one of the most popular of all American concert works.

Another notable composition is The Blue Danube, a waltz by Austrian composer Johann Strauss the Younger that epitomizes the symphonic richness and variety of his dance music. Created in 1867, it has become the best-known of his many dance pieces and earned him acclaim as the "waltz king."

## Film Overview
The Count is Charlie Chaplin's fifth film for Mutual Film Corporation in 1916. Released on September 4, it co-starred Eric Campbell and Edna Purviance.

## Plot
The tailor's handyman burns a count's trousers while ironing them and is fired. His superior discovers a note explaining the count can't attend a party, and dresses up like one to take his place. Chaplin also goes to the residence hosting the party, but runs into the tailor. They both then struggle to win the fair maiden, Miss Moneybags.

## Production
The film was produced by Lone Star Corporation and distributed by Mutual Film Corporation. Writer/Director: Charles Chaplin, and cinematography was by Roland H. Totheroh and W.C. Foster.

The film is a classic example of Chaplin's silent comedy work from his prolific Mutual period.

Western fiction is a genre of literature set in the American Old West frontier and typically set from the late eighteenth to the late nineteenth century. Well-known writers of Western fiction include Zane Grey from the early 20th century and Louis L'Amour from the mid-20th century.

Westerns often stress the harshness of the wilderness and frequently set the action in an arid, desolate landscape of deserts and mountains, with the vast landscape often playing an important role and presenting a "mythic vision of the plains and deserts of the American West". Many Westerns use a stock plot of depicting a crime, then showing the pursuit of the wrongdoer, ending in revenge and retribution, which is often dispensed through a shootout or quick draw duel.

Regarding the genre's popularity, the genre's popularity peaked in the 1960s, due in part to the shuttering of many pulp magazines, the popularity of televised Westerns, and the rise of the spy novel, with readership beginning to drop off in the mid- to late 1970s and reaching a new low in the 2000s.

## Woody Allen

Woody Allen (born Allan Stewart Konigsberg; November 30, 1935) is an American filmmaker, actor, writer, and comedian. He is known for bittersweet comic films containing elements of parody, slapstick, and the absurd.

### Career Highlights

After writing, directing, and starring in a string of slapstick comedies, such as Take the Money and Run (1969), Bananas (1971), Sleeper (1973), and Love and Death (1975), he directed his seminal work Annie Hall (1977). The film received widespread acclaim and won four Academy Awards: Best Picture, Best Director and Best Original Screenplay, and Best Actress for Keaton.

Allen has since directed many films set in New York City, including Manhattan (1979), Hannah and Her Sisters (1986), and Crimes and Misdemeanors (1989).

### Directorial Style and Impact

Allen became one of the most productive filmmakers of his time, turning out almost a film a year throughout his career. Allen has received numerous accolades, including the most wins and nominations for the Academy Award for Best Original Screenplay (3 and 16 respectively).
